title: The Godfather
synopsis: A wedding. A horse's head. A war between five families. You're the youngest son. The family business is, finally, calling you.

nodes.text: Long Beach in August. Connie's veil keeps snagging on the folding chairs and the band will not stop playing. No Sicilian refuses a request on his daughter's wedding day, so the line outside the study runs the length of the hall: a baker, an undertaker, a man who wants a part in a picture. You stay out on the lawn in your uniform, telling Kay which cousins she can safely ignore.

choices.consequence: You keep your back to the house and your hand on the back of her chair. Out here you are a decorated soldier with a college girl. Inside, you are the youngest son.
You stand where you can watch your father's hands while he listens. You are not conducting business. You are learning the grammar of it.

nodes.text: Kay asks about the man by the cake with the wet face, the one who came out of the study looking rescued. So you tell her the whole thing: the contract, the bandleader, the two men who went along to explain it. You watch her decide it must be a story about somebody else's family. Then you say the sentence you have been rehearsing since the Pacific. That's them. That isn't me.

choices.consequence: You believe every word of it on the way out of your mouth. You will never afterward be able to locate the exact afternoon it stopped being true.
Some part of you is already adding a clause you don't say out loud. Kay hears the sentence. You hear the clause, and you hear it for years.

nodes.text: The Turk comes with figures and a Tattaglia standing behind him: financing, judges, protection, a return your father cannot argue with on paper. Your father listens the way he listens to everyone, hands folded, then says his friends in the courts would stop being friends over narcotics. It is a refusal wearing the clothes of a regret. Sonny opens his mouth in front of a stranger and asks one question too many.

choices.consequence: You accept that the old man has read a room correctly for forty years. He has. He has also just been informed, very courteously, that he is finished.
You say nothing at the table and a great deal in the kitchen afterward. Nobody in that house wants strategy from the son who enlisted against orders.

nodes.text: You bring oranges at ten at night and the lobby is wrong: no men on the door, nobody on the stairs, one nurse irritated at being disturbed after hours. Your father is alone in the room with tubes in him, breathing. You count the corridors. Down on the street a car slows and does not park. Your hands stay perfectly steady, and you notice that about yourself, and file it.

choices.consequence: You roll his bed into another room and put Enzo the baker on the steps with a hand inside his coat. The car keeps going. You are immediately, alarmingly good at this.
You find a payphone and spend ninety seconds explaining the situation to Sonny. Ninety seconds is all you have. You never make that kind of call again.

nodes.text: McCluskey turns up with an escort and a story about a raid, and when you tell him plainly where his men went he swings with no wind-up at all. Your jaw goes sideways. You come to on the hospital steps with your mouth full of blood and a police captain's shield six inches from your eye. Nobody in your family has ever seen your face broken before tonight.

choices.consequence: You spend the wired weeks doing arithmetic instead of shouting. When you finally speak at the meeting the room goes quiet, because it is a plan and not a temper.
You keep it behind your teeth for a month while wire holds your jaw shut. Rage held that long stops resembling rage. It begins to resemble judgment.

nodes.text: The Bronx, red tablecloth, veal that nobody there will finish. Clemenza has taped a clean revolver behind the tank in the washroom, no serial, small calibre, loud. Solozzo talks Sicilian across the table so the captain can't follow. You excuse yourself, you come back, you sit down, and for two entire seconds you let a man explain his position to you with your hand under the cloth.

choices.consequence: You stand up and after that the room is only noise and plaster dust. You walk out exactly as instructed, let the gun drop from your fingers, and stop being a civilian.
You think about going straight past the table and out onto the street. The thought survives one step. Then you sit, because Sonny's name is on the other side of it.

nodes.text: Corleone: a village that shares your name, two shepherds with shotguns walking wherever you walk, light coming off the stone until New York feels like a rumour somebody told you. You learn the names of trees and the price of oil. Outside Vitelli's you see a girl walking with her cousins, and something goes through you that the shepherds laugh about and have an old word for.

choices.consequence: You sit in her father's cafe with your terrible Sicilian and ask permission like a schoolboy. For one season you are somebody's husband and nothing else, and it nearly holds.
You keep to the wall and watch her pass, telling yourself a man with a warrant has no business handing anyone his name. You hand it to her three weeks later.

nodes.text: She has been learning to drive and is proud of it. You are on the steps and she is behind the wheel of the little Alfa laughing at you through the windscreen, and Fabrizio is walking out through the gate too quickly. You are still shouting her name when the car goes up. Afterward you stand in the heat by the burning frame, and something inside you closes and does not open again.

choices.consequence: You spend a year learning where Fabrizio went. Years later, when you finally settle it, the act costs you nothing whatsoever, and the nothing is the frightening part.
You bury her and stop saying her name, even privately. Whatever grief was owed gets converted into something more useful somewhere over the Atlantic.

nodes.text: A year of not answering letters, then Kay in a schoolyard in New Hampshire with children lining up in twos behind her. You tell her you work for your father now. You tell her the family will be entirely legitimate inside five years. You ask her to marry you and to trust you, and you leave the Bronx out of it, and you keep leaving it out for twenty years.

choices.text: Promise the family will go legitimate
choices.consequence: You give her a number and a date and she writes both down somewhere permanent in herself. She will hold you to that timetable out loud, at dinner, in front of people.
You refuse to name a year, which you privately class as honesty. She marries you on a promise vague enough that you can both go on believing it.

nodes.text: The causeway toll booth, his change in his hand, men waiting behind the barriers with Thompsons. They keep firing well past any reason to. Bonasera is asked to make him presentable and cannot manage it. Out in the garden your father sits with a glass of wine he never lifts and says the thing he has never said to you, which is that he wanted something else entirely for you.

choices.consequence: You step forward because there is nobody left standing. Tom isn't Sicilian, Fredo can't be trusted with a car, and the old man has no blood left to spend.
You let Tom keep the title and run the whole thing from the chair beside his. Everyone who needs to know who decides things already knows.

nodes.text: He calls the Five Families to a bank boardroom, long table, no weapons, and asks for a truce, and asks for it as a father rather than a Don. Barzini and Tattaglia grant it, because an old man's request is cheap. He surrenders the narcotics fight to buy you a safe passage home. From the wall you work out who actually arranged everything, and the answer is not Tattaglia.

choices.consequence: You count eyes and note which men glance at Barzini before they answer. Your father spends the last of his strength purchasing you an amnesty he cannot afford.
You take the chair at his shoulder so the table can see the succession. Half the men in that room start pricing you before the coffee arrives.

nodes.text: Tom lays it out in the office with the blinds down: the union in Vegas, the requests for a meeting, who is offering to broker what. Your father told you plainly that whoever came to arrange the sit-down with Barzini would be the one who sold you. Tessio has now come to you with a place and a time. Tessio taught Sonny how to hold a pistol.

choices.consequence: You have his route watched for six days before you allow yourself to accept it. Certainty is worth the delay. You need to do this without heat in your hands.
You decide inside a minute, because the waiting would only be for your own comfort, and comfort is not something the family can currently afford to buy.

nodes.text: The church is English, the priest is Irish, and Kay's people come down from New Hampshire and stand very politely at the edges of the reception. Your father dances with your wife and she laughs at whatever he tells her. There are men at that party whose deaths you have already scheduled. You keep the seating chart in your head and your hand flat against her back.

choices.consequence: You give your father the first dance, the head table, the old songs, the whole afternoon. It is the last completely good day that yard ever hosts.
You work the room while the band plays, reading who drifts toward whom. Kay says afterward that you look far away in every photograph, and she is right.

nodes.text: He is retired now to tomato stakes and a watering can, an old man in a cardigan losing an argument with a garden sprayer. He tells you Barzini will come at you through somebody close and trusted, and to expect the approach, and not to be surprised by the face. Then he plays monster with your boy among the plants, orange peel in his teeth, and goes down between the rows.

choices.text: Promise him to honor the family
choices.consequence: You give him your word in the yard while he is still holding the sprayer. He says he is proud of you. He means one thing by it and you accept another.
You promise yourself privately that you'll be cleaner than he was. You keep that promise about the paperwork and break it about every single person.

nodes.text: The kitchen table, the lists, the coffee going grey. Barzini. Tattaglia. Cuneo. Stracci. Moe Greene out in the desert. Clemenza's men, Neri in a stolen uniform, a revolving door, a hotel massage table, an elevator with a good sightline. You put all of it inside one hour on the morning Connie has asked you to stand godfather to her son, in front of two hundred witnesses.

choices.consequence: You go down the list without pausing once and initial the whole page. Tom watches you do it and never again offers you an opinion on that subject.
You hold one name back overnight, just to feel what it feels like. It feels like weakness with better manners, and by morning you have written him back in.

nodes.text: Cold water, Latin, the baby furious in your arms, Connie beaming at you from the second pew. The priest asks whether you renounce Satan and all his works and all his empty promises, and you answer him in a clear steady voice, and across the city elevator doors are opening. You have never been calmer. A godfather's one duty, they tell you, is the child's soul.

choices.consequence: You give the priest the responses as though the words were still available to you. Nothing moves in your face. Nothing has moved in your face for a long time.
You say it the way you'd sign a lease. Somewhere behind your ribs you note the precise moment you stopped bothering to lie to yourself as well as to everyone else.

nodes.text: You tell Carlo he's out of the family and to take a plane, and that all you want is the name of whoever set Sonny up at the causeway. He gives you Barzini fast, sweating through his collar, relieved to be trading. You tell him his punishment is exile. Then you put him in the car with Clemenza and hold Connie's screaming out of your mind for the length of one cigarette.

choices.consequence: You file it under Sonny, where the columns balance exactly. The arithmetic works so cleanly that you find yourself using it again on other people later.
You decline to construct a reason at all. That is the afternoon you discover you no longer need one, and the discovery turns out to be a great convenience.

nodes.text: Connie comes apart in the hallway and says all of it in front of your wife: the baby, the beatings, the car, the toll booth. Kay waits until the house has emptied and then asks you straight out whether it's true about Carlo. You tell her never to ask about the business. She asks once anyway. So you give her this one, and you look at her while you hand it over.

choices.consequence: You keep your voice gentle and your eyes level and give her exactly the answer she needs in order to stay. She takes it and pours you a drink with unsteady hands.
You make it short and flat with no softening anywhere in it. She believes you for as long as it takes to walk to the study door, which is roughly four seconds.

nodes.text: Clemenza and Neri and Rocco are waiting in the office, and one after another they take your hand and bend over it and say Don Corleone, a title that until recently belonged to an old man with a watering can. Through the doorway your wife is standing in the hall holding the drink she just made you. Neri crosses the room without being asked and shuts the door on her.

choices.consequence: You watch it swing closed and you do not put out a hand to stop it. Twenty years on, in another house entirely, you can still describe her face at that moment.
You are already listening to Clemenza. The click behind you registers somewhere and gets filed with everything else you have decided not to turn around and look at.

nodes.text: Nevada now: a compound on a lake, attorneys instead of buttonmen, a gaming licence pending, a senator's aide returning your calls within the hour. The men who kissed your hand are dead or retired to Florida with bad hearts. Your son will be told his grandfather imported olive oil, and it will be technically true, and he will believe it because you built the entire apparatus so he could.

choices.consequence: You have said it aloud so many times that it has acquired the weight of a fact. Everyone who could have contradicted the sentence is under a stone.
You run the honest version once, alone, late, with the lake black outside the glass. Then you put it away, because there is a meeting at nine.

nodes.text: The chair is his. The desk is his. The drapes still hold his cigars faintly, four years on. There is a photograph of him at the corner of the blotter in a cheap frame he bought himself. You sit down, and it fits, and it fit the first time you tried it. Everything from here you choose on purpose. There is no Solozzo left to blame it on.

choices.consequence: You pick the version of yourself that requires no reasons. It is the most efficient man in the room, and eventually it is the only man in the room.
You resolve to be a Don who keeps his word, which is achievable, and which is not remotely the same thing as being a decent man.
You choose neither and let the work decide for you, one small reasonable ruling at a time, until you look up at a stranger you never once sat down and selected.

nodes.text: You rule for thirty years and nothing moves between New York and the desert without your permission. Kay takes the children east in a year you barely register at the time. The family becomes quiet, enormous and feared, exactly as designed. At the end you are a man in a good chair in a room with nobody in it, doing the work, because the work is the only thing that never asked you for something you couldn't give it.

It takes you twenty years to deliver what you promised her in five. Casinos, then hotels, then land, then banks, then a foundation with your father's name embossed on the letterhead. Your grandchildren attend schools that ask nothing about where the first money came from, and one of them stands for the Senate on a platform of clean government. Somewhere in there the history stops being a crime and becomes a founding story, told at dinner, to laughter.

You get old in Nevada and then, improbably, in a garden, on your knees in the dirt with a bad back and a stubborn sprayer. A granddaughter with Connie's chin drags you down the rows demanding the names of things. You end up gentler than you set out to be, which was never the plan and cannot now be undone. Nobody hands you a thing for it. You take it anyway, quietly, as the last small victory available.
